result.abstractText: New catalytic manifolds that challenge existing boundaries for synthesis and sustainable manufacturing are notoriously difficult to implement<sup>1</sup>, particularly for catalytic paradigms based on metals which lack access to the fundamental processes that underpin many established d-block mechanistic pathways (e.g. oxidative addition and reductive elimination). The widespread exploitation of systems based on main-group elements therefore requires alternative elementary steps to effect turnover. Herein, we demonstrate a new catalytic platform for nucleophilic fluorination, which exploits a complex based on calcium (the fifth most Earth-abundant element) as the fluoride delivery vehicle. The key intermediate is a calcium-fluoride complex featuring a terminal Ca-F interaction, a unique structural geometry enabled by a highly sterically encumbered dianionic ligand-scaffold. Twisting two atomic layers produces a geometric moiré pattern but bonding-induced interfacial reconstruction fundamentally transforms this into an ordered dislocation network-a distinction obscured in weakly bonded van der Waals systems. Although in-plane topological vortex nanostructures arising from twisting-induced lateral strain modulation have been linked to periodic moiré patterns in freestanding perovskite layers<sup>1-3</sup> and 2D bilayers<sup>4</sup>, their coupling to the interfacial dislocation network in twisted layers remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate that twisted freestanding SrTiO<sub>3</sub> (STO) layers undergo interfacial reconstruction into a network of screw dislocations, accompanied by the emergence of in-plane topological vortices. Unlike in previous reports, these vortices are associated with the dislocation network rather than with geometric moiré patterns

The Amazon rainforest is a cornerstone of regional and global carbon cycling<sup>1</sup> and is widely regarded and modelled as a perennially evergreen ecosystem<sup>2,3</sup>. This prevailing view, however, masks substantial fine-scale variation in leaf phenology, limiting our capacity to predict ecosystem responses to climate change. Here by combining 10-m Sentinel-2 observations with machine learning, we uncover pervasive, spatially structured seasonal deciduousness across the basin. In 70.0% of the Amazon, leaf shedding precedes leaf flushing by at least 3 months, creating pronounced asynchrony between deciduousness and greenness seasonality, whereas the remainder shows near-synchronous phenology. Current understanding of the host tissue response to solid tumours is largely based on investigations of tumour types in isolation<sup>1</sup>. Given the breadth and diversity of human tumour pathology and contributions of tumour microenvironment (TME) cells to disease progression, pan-cancer analysis is needed to bridge major themes of stromal and immune cell evolution. To date, however, efforts to compare the TME response across cancers have been limited in scope<sup>2,3</sup>. Here we conduct a comprehensive pan-cancer analysis by algorithmically screening thousands of publicly available single-cell transcriptomic datasets for stromal and immune signatures across species and tissue types. We demonstrate conserved hallmarks of host cell transcriptional programming in response to malignancy across 42 cancer types in more than 2,000 human and mouse tumour samples. Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have emerged as a promising photovoltaic technology, with efficiencies rapidly approaching those of established crystalline-silicon solar cells. Further efficiency gains, however, are increasingly limited by charge extraction and recombination at the interface between the perovskite absorber and the electron-transport layer. Interfacial modifiers are widely used to suppress these losses, yet many conventional ammonium-based modifiers are weakly electronically coupled to the perovskite surface and can introduce barriers to electron extraction <sup>1-5</sup>. Here we realize electronically coupled heterointerfaces by introducing a family of heteroatom-containing, fully conjugated formamidinium interfacial modulators, establishing band-edge-extending conjugated heterointerfaces that overcome the bottleneck of inefficient interfacial electron transfer. A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction<sup>1-5</sup>. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA-mCherry)<sup>6</sup> with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH))<sup>7,8</sup> to establish TransA-MERFISH. As a primary port of pathogen entry, the intestinal mucosa has developed a sophisticated set of defences to ward off infections. Investigating the human-specific intestinal barrier responses to pathogens is limited by the lack of models integrating the necessary architectural complexity with an autologous immune compartment<sup>1</sup>. Here we developed engineered barrier models of the human small intestine and colon combining a multilineage epithelium, mucus layer, accessible microbial compartment and autologous tissue-resident immune cells. These tissues recapitulate morphological and functional properties that are region specific and compare with those of the native organ. Islands account for a disproportionate share of global biodiversity<sup>1</sup>, yet insects, including invaluable pollinators such as bees<sup>2</sup>, remain underrepresented in island biogeography research<sup>3</sup>. Here we present a global checklist of island bees, recording 4,147 species across 305 islands. Although islands comprise only about 6% of the Earth's land area, they support around 20% of known global bee diversity, and 42% of insular species are endemic, making up around 8% of all known bee species. Island bee species richness peaks at mid-latitudes (at least in the Northern Hemisphere), mirroring continental trends<sup>4</sup>. Native richness increases with island area and declines with isolation, consistent with patterns in other taxa<sup>5</sup>. Position information underpins many modern technologies, from navigation and timing to authentication and critical infrastructure<sup>1-3</sup>. However, classical methods of proving that information originates from a particular position are vulnerable to spoofing<sup>4-6</sup>. This limitation can be overcome with quantum technologies<sup>7-16</sup>, but current protocols rely on trust in quantum hardware that can be undermined<sup>17,18</sup>, or require quantum computers and bounds on adversarial computation<sup>19</sup>. Nevertheless, there has been considerable interest in experimental demonstrations, and aspects of these protocols have been implemented<sup>20-22</sup>. Cavity quantum electrodynamics<sup>1</sup> with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light-matter interactions<sup>2,3</sup> and exploring many-body phenomena<sup>4,5</sup>. In particular, superradiance<sup>6</sup>-arising from collective quantum interference among emitters-has been explored as a route to ultrastable continuous radiation<sup>7</sup>. However, engineering superradiance in the time domain to realize periodic pulsed sources or frequency combs remains largely unexplored. Here we investigate the non-equilibrium many-body dynamics of a driven spin ensemble coupled with an on-chip superconducting resonator and uncover a dynamical phase transition from continuous-wave to periodic pulsed superradiant emission. Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration<sup>1,2</sup>. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. Hominin fossils and genetic evidence indicate that several hominin populations occupied East and Southeast Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene epoch<sup>1-10</sup>. Homo erectus fossils remain scarce in southern China and mainland Southeast Asia<sup>4,8,11</sup>. Here we report nine newly discovered late Middle Pleistocene hominin teeth from the Naxian and Baxian caves at the Chongzuo study area, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, southern China, dated to around 324-184 thousand years ago<sup>12</sup>. Palaeoproteomics reveals the presence of an endogenous dental proteome in all five hominin teeth studied molecularly. Four teeth contain a derived H. erectus substitution in ameloblastin that to date has been observed only in older Middle Pleistocene H. erectus specimens from China<sup>13</sup>. Homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago<sup>1</sup> to 108 thousand years ago (ka)<sup>2</sup>. Despite this, there are still large gaps in our understanding of the adaptation capabilities of this species and the extent of its persistence in China. Assumptions over ecological preferences based on the Trinil<sup>3</sup>, Sangiran<sup>4</sup> and Ngandong<sup>2</sup> (in Java) open woodland-grassland mosaics have persisted, combined with limited direct stable carbon isotope measurements in Asia. Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus<sup>5</sup>, found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars<sup>1,2</sup>. This is theorized to happen through common envelope evolution (CEE)<sup>3</sup>, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag<sup>4,5</sup>. Metabolic disorders such as diabetes mellitus are global health crises driven by metabolic imbalance, chronic inflammation and dysfunction of the neuroimmune axis<sup>1-3</sup>. Electroceuticals targeting the autonomic nervous system have shown anti-inflammatory effects, yet existing systems lack the metabolic interoceptive feedback to fully restore immune-metabolic homeostasis<sup>4-9</sup>. Here we report an artificial neuroimmune axis (NeuroAxis) as a closed-loop immunomodulatory therapy for treating metabolic diseases. Analogous to its biological counterpart, NeuroAxis is solely powered by endogenous glucose, operating without batteries or wireless power transfer. It emulates the vagal reflex through closed-loop neuromodulation with metabolic interoceptive feedback. Corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets are central to climate action, but they often fall short of driving meaningful business transformation. Despite progress in standardization, current target-setting approaches remain weakened by methodological problems, including inaccurate emissions accounting, excluded emissions sources and limited comparability across companies. More importantly, many corporate targets are disconnected from the real-world sectoral transitions required to meet the Paris Agreement's temperature goal. Drawing on evidence from four editions of the Corporate Climate Responsibility Monitor and recent literature, we argue that target-setting frameworks should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains. Cells dynamically assemble actin into branched networks to push on their environment during cell migration, endocytosis or the maintenance of cell-cell contact<sup>1</sup>. These networks are among the stiffest found in the cytoskeleton and can generate large pushing stresses against stationary obstacles<sup>2-5</sup>. When grown against a controlled opposing stress in an atomic force microscope<sup>6</sup> or inside the cell<sup>7</sup>, branched networks alter their own architecture to adapt their compressional stiffness to their environment, but the underpinnings of their mechanics and adaptability are unclear. Here we show that their high density and low connectivity place them outside the scope of standard elastic network models for actin. Gene transcription within the viral core is a distinctive feature of poxvirus replication. Following entry into the cytoplasm, the poxvirus core dissociates from the lateral bodies and undergoes expansion, functioning as a compartment for early transcription<sup>1</sup>. However, how molecules are exchanged between the viral core and the host cytoplasm remains poorly understood. Here, using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging, we determine the structures of the portal complex and its central pore on the vaccinia virus core at 6.7 Å and 4.4 Å resolution, respectively. Guided by structural predictions and experimental density, we identify three viral proteins, E8, E6 and L3, as the principal components of the pore and construct a structural model of their organization. X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP) is an adult-onset movement disorder predominantly affecting males of Filipino descent. It is caused by the insertion of a SINE-variable number of tandem repeat (VNTR)-Alu subfamily F (SVA_F) retrotransposon in the TATA-box binding protein-associated factor 1 (TAF1) gene. A barrier to XDP research has been the lack of animal models. Here, we introduce a conditional humanized XDP mouse model harboring a hybrid mouse-human Taf1/TAF1 gene (hyTAF1) containing the pathogenic SVA_F. We activated hyTAF1 in Nestin<sup>+</sup> cells and found the resulting XDP male mice recapitulate features of human XDP, including severe motor impairment and striatal atrophy. Transcriptomic, histological, and electron microscopy analyses revealed a reduction in oligodendrocyte-lineage cells and myelin disruption. Anopheles stephensi, a malaria-transmitting mosquito, has invaded Africa and rapidly adapts to the high temperatures in urban settings. However, the molecular basis of its thermal adaptation remains unclear. Here, we identified a variant of a 5-kb deletion in the circadian clock gene timeless (tim<sup>-5kb</sup>) that rose to high frequency after 3 years of rearing at high laboratory temperatures. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease. Although current immunotherapies control relapses, they have limited impact on progression, which might reflect incomplete access to or modulation of compartmentalized CNS inflammation. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells can infiltrate tissues, but their ability to access and eliminate immune cells residing in the CNS remains elusive. We report the treatment of five individuals with progressive or relapsing-remitting MS with autologous CD19 CAR T cells to assess safety-relevant aspects, CNS bioavailability, and compartment-specific effects. The intervention induces remodeling of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) B cell pool, with a sustained reduction in CSF humoral biomarkers. Once labeled the "Dark Ages" of Anatolian prehistory, the Chalcolithic period (c. 6000-3000 BCE) was characterized by drastically reduced settlement densities compared with the preceding Neolithic and the succeeding Bronze Ages, a change interpreted as population decline. Using 44 new genomes combined with published data, we find no evidence for a population reduction. The genetic evidence instead suggests that populations in Chalcolithic Anatolia were increasingly mobile and/or growing in size while receiving gene flow from eastern regions (e.g., East Anatolia and the South Caucasus) through a 3,000-year-long admixture process. We propose that genetic and archaeological evidence may be reconciled by hypothesizing the presence of communities with dispersed and mobile lifeways that are mostly invisible to archaeology. The ability of vertebrates to conquer land is attributed to innovations in respiration and locomotion. However, land adaptation profoundly reshaped mucosal surfaces such as the skin, the main interface between hosts and the environment. To adapt to land, African lungfish annually remodel their skin, forming a cocoon. Here, we report the discovery of a small pore-forming toxin in African lungfish, Protop-CrTX-A, with no other vertebrate counterpart that is sufficient to drive epithelial morphogenesis transcriptional programs. In free-swimming lungfish, goblet cells secrete Protop-CrTX-A into the mucus. During estivation, this niche is replaced by a mucin-low/basal epithelial niche, adjacent to a granulocyte immune niche that becomes the predominant source of Protop-CrTX-A in the estivated skin. Understanding respiratory virus transmission requires integrating pathogen genomic data with detailed epidemiological context. We analyzed >85,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes linked to epidemiological data collected in Massachusetts from November 2021 to January 2023. Collected in 666 settings, including schools, colleges, and skilled nursing facilities, this dataset enabled direct comparison of within-setting transmission to community-wide risk. Elevated transmission was concentrated in specific age-defined subpopulations-older adolescents in schools, undergraduates in colleges, and residents in nursing facilities-with little additional risk among other groups, notably including staff. Young adults, particularly in colleges, played a disproportionate role in spread, and new viral lineages consistently expanded first within this group. Human retrotransposon insertions are often associated with diseases. Regarding neurodegenerative X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), a human-specific SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) subfamily F retrotransposon was inserted in intron 32 of the TAF1 gene. Here, we genomically rewrote a portion of the mouse Taf1 allele with the corresponding 78-kb XDP patient-derived TAF1 allele. In mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), the presence of the intronic SVA-rather than the hybrid gene structure-reduces hyTAF1 (hybrid TAF1 mRNA) levels. This leads to transcriptional downregulation of genes with TATA boxes enriched in their promoters and triggers apoptosis. Chromatin and transcriptome profiling revealed that intronic SVAs are actively transcribed, forming barriers that likely impede transcription elongation. RNA viruses form membraneless condensates in host cells to drive replication, but whether these compartments regulate host RNAs remains unclear. Using multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)-based subcellular transcriptomics, we quantified cellular mRNA recruitment into Ebola virus condensates under basal and interferon (IFN)-stimulated states. We find that, in the basal state, cellular RNAs with minimally folded coding regions are selectively recruited. Under IFN stimulation, however, IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) with structured 3' UTRs concentrate in viral condensates. We find that both RNA structural features are conserved in the viral genome and support its retention in condensates.
